To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) including twins and sibling pairs in genetic association studies can substantially increase the power of the study to detect a true association, and (2) sampling twins and sibling pairs that have discordant genotypes is the most powerful design.

the use of discordant twins and sibling pairs in association studies is a powerful design that can substantially increase the power of an association study over designs that use unrelated subjects or monozygotic twin pairs, particularly when the disease of interest is rare.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing efficient designs for testing genetic hypotheses that consider twins and/or siblings with discordant genotypic data at the locus (loci) of interest.
developing efficient designs that consider twins and siblings with discordant genotypic information in genetic association studies.
the development of efficient designs for genetic association testing that consider twins and/or sibling pairs discordant in their genotypes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of discordant twins and siblings in association studies is a powerful approach to testing genetic hypotheses and that the use of existing family‐based cohorts in association studies is an efficient and cost‐effective way of pursuing such studies.

the results of this study suggest that a combination of the following three factors is important for the development of the most effective and efficient genetic association study designs: 1) a well‐designed study that considers the appropriate population, the appropriate disease and/or phenotype, the appropriate genotypes and/or genetic variants, and the appropriate statistical methods, 2) an appropriate sample size and 3) the appropriate study design, i.e., the appropriate use of family or twin‐discordant designs.
, for any particular disease, it is difficult to know whether a given genetic association is truly causal or not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, from a statistical perspective, it makes sense to include twins or siblings discordant for genotyped loci in association studies.

, if one is going to test the association between a genetic variation and a subclinical phenotype that is expensive to measure (e.g. a molecular or histological phenotype) and if the genetic variation is known or suspected to be rare, it may be advantageous to use twins or sibling pairs that are discordant for genotypic information as the basis of the association study.
the inclusion of twins and/or discordant sibling pairs into association studies, when possible, can substantially increase statistical power.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inclusion of twins and sibling pairs discordant at a particular locus (or locii) can substantially increase the power to detect an association with respect a given phenotype.
the inclusion of twins or siblings with discordant genotyped at the locus being tested in association studies can substantially increase the power of such studies.

the inclusion of twins and siblings discordant for a particular genetic variation in a case‐control association study can increase the power to detect a true association between a particular genetic variation and disease risk.
